title: Luther on vocation
hookLine: Luther taught that ordinary work, a milkmaid's or a cobbler's, can be a holy calling
last: IDLENESS IS THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.

lines: A COBBLER, A SMITH, A FARMER.
cards: A cobbler hammers a heel onto a boot. A smith pumps the bellows. A farmer walks behind the plow.
Ask a churchgoer in their town who has a calling from God, and the answer might point up the hill, to the monastery, or to the priest at the altar.
Then a monk named Martin Luther, a teacher of the Bible in Germany, starts saying something that sounds almost backward. The cobbler at his bench, he says, is doing God's work too. Not after hours.

teach.h: NO HIGHER RUNG FOR THE CLOISTER.
teach.b: Vocation means a calling. First, the argument. Luther objected to the idea that people in religious orders stood on a higher spiritual level than everyone else.

In an open letter to the German nobility, he wrote that a cobbler, a smith and a farmer each has the work and office of his trade, and yet all of them are consecrated priests and bishops, through baptism.
Second, the verse he leaned on.

Paul writes, in the King James Bible, "Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called." Luther read calling there to include a person's ordinary station: parent, servant, ruler, maker of things.

teach.h: GOD MILKS THE COWS, IT'S SAID.
teach.b: A line often credited to Luther says that God himself milks the cows through the vocation of the milkmaid. It's hard to find those exact words in his writings, so treat it as a saying people pass on in his name.
But it catches what he taught: the daily work that feeds and clothes and serves your neighbor is where God is at work. Fourth, what Christians made of it.
Lutheran and other Protestant churches built on this idea of vocation.
Catholic teaching today also speaks of the vocation of lay people in ordinary work and family life, alongside the calling to priesthood and religious life.

teach.h: CHURCHES SAY IT THEIR OWN WAY.
teach.b: Churches say it in their own ways.
And the idea has traveled outside churches too: what if this job, this shift, this kitchen, is more than a way to pay rent? What if it's a calling?

how: Lutheran and other Protestant churches teach vocation as serving God and neighbor in ordinary work and family life; Catholic teaching also speaks of the vocation of lay people alongside priesthood and religious life.

o: a calling, which Luther found in ordinary work too
a calling that belongs only to priests and monks
a job skill you train for at a trade school

games.q: Luther and his callings — tap the pairs.
p: each has the work of his trade

s: Luther taught that only priests and monks had a calling
he argued the opposite: the cobbler and the farmer have callings too.
the milkmaid line is easy to find, word for word, in Luther's writings
it's hard to find; treat it as a saying passed on in his name.
Catholic teaching today speaks of a vocation for lay people too
alongside the calling to priesthood and religious life.

games.q: you're a cobbler in Luther's town. you want to serve God better. Luther's teaching says…
o: close the shop and join a monastery.
your trade is already a calling: serve your neighbor through it.
give your earnings to the church and stop working.
games.why: Luther wrote that the cobbler, the smith and the farmer each has the work and office of his trade, and all are consecrated priests. the shop is the calling.

practice: Name your own stations, one at a time, the way Luther read calling: son or daughter, parent, coworker, neighbor, student, friend.

Choose the one that feels least holy and picture one ordinary moment in it today; you don't have to call it holy, just let it count as yours. If you pray, you can bring that station and its work into your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Vocation. A calling. Luther argued that ordinary work, the cobbler's and the farmer's, can be a holy calling, not only the priest's or the monk's. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my calling. Even the station that feels least holy. Day eight hundred ninety-one counts.
